docs.title: Welcome to Celldega's Documentation
docs.text:
Celldega Landscape visualization of a human skin cancer Xenium dataset obtained from 10X Genomics.

Celldega is a spatial analysis and visualization library that is being developed by the Spatial Technology Platform at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. This project enables researchers to easily visualize large ST datasets (e.g., datasets with >100M transcripts) alongside single-cell and spatial analysis notebook workflows (e.g., sverse tools and novel spatial analysis approaches).

  • Getting Started
  • Installation
  • GitHub Repository

docs.title: Atera
docs.text: Visualize 10x Atera whole-transcriptome data in Celldega. The Atera Kidney Landscape-Clustergram tutorial explores 399,120 cells and over 1 billion transcripts in a human kidney section with linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Yearbook views, including cell-type composition around glomeruli.

docs.title: Visium HD Colorectal Cancer Tutorial Video
docs.text: This video shows how to link a Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich to analyze a Visium HD human colorectal cancer dataset. Follow along in the Visium HD Human CRC Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich tutorial.

docs.title: 3D Developing Mouse Brain
docs.text: Explore 3.8 million cells from 43 aligned Xenium sections of an E15.5 mouse brain as a 3D CellCloud. See the Broad-Allen Dev Mouse Brain E15.5 Viz tutorial.

docs.title: bioRxiv Preprint
docs.text: Our preprint, Celldega: Integrated Toolkit for Visualization and Analysis of Spatial Data, is available on bioRxiv.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
Celldega is named after a bodega, a small shop with all the essentials that is part of the fabric of a neighborhood.

Celldega is open source and available on GitHub.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text: Celldega visualizations are designed notebook-first — used as widgets locally or in the cloud — but they aren't limited to a notebook: they can also run as a stand-alone JavaScript library on any webpage.

docs.title: Notebook environments
docs.text:
• Local Jupyter — JupyterLab or Jupyter Notebook running on your own machine, following the standard Installation and Getting Started guides.
  • Cloud notebook services — hosted notebook environments such as Manifold, Google Colab, Marimo, and Molab. Celldega installs like any other PyPI package (pip install celldega); widget rendering depends on the service supporting the Jupyter Widgets protocol.

docs.title: Standalone web usage
docs.text:
Celldega's visualizations also run outside of a notebook entirely, as a stand-alone JavaScript library against publicly hosted data — see the JavaScript API. The Gallery is a collection of such stand-alone web pages showcasing datasets across technologies (Xenium, CosMx, Visium HD, and more).

Support for a desktop Celldega app is planned for a future release.

docs.title: STP Segmentation Usage on Terra.bio
docs.text:
The following guide assumes some familiarity with Terra, WDL, and the basics of running workflows in a cloud environment.

Click here for a brief overview of Terra, and here for a brief overview of WDL.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The stp_segmentation_wdl GitHub repository contains WDL workflows for running cell segmentation tasks, utilizing Python scripts for preprocessing, segmentation, and postprocessing. These workflows are designed for compatibility with Cromwell, the WDL execution engine, and are ready to be deployed on Terra.

docs.title: Repository Contents
docs.text:
The repository includes:

  • Main WDL Files: Defines the workflow, tasks, and their dependencies.

  • Task WDL Files: Breaks workflows into specific steps, e.g., image preprocessing, running segmentation algorithms like Cellpose, Instanseg, etc., and result handling.

  • Python Scripts: Found in the repository's source folder (or referenced in WDL tasks). These scripts handle computational tasks like tiling, segmentation, merging tiling results and assignment of transcripts.

  • Docker Files: Predefined images (hosted on Docker Hub) to ensure reproducibility across environments.

docs.title: Terra Workspace Setup
docs.text:
• Access the GitHub Repository

Visit stp_segmentation_wdl GitHub repository and review the README for guides, specific details about prerequisites, and local workflow execution.

  • Set Up a Terra Workspace

Log in to Terra. If a dedicated workspace does not already exist, create one by navigating to the Workspaces tab and clicking the plus (+) icon next to the Workspaces heading. More details can be found here.

  • Workspaces
  • Import the Workflow

In the workspace, go to the Workflows tab. Click Find a Workflow, search for stp_segmentation_wdl, and import the appropriate version. More details can be found here.

  • Workflows
  • Input Configuration

Use the intuitive Terra workflow submission GUI to provide relevant WDL inputs or create an inputs.json file based on your dataset. Key inputs include:

  • Image Data: Cloud storage paths to the images (e.g., .tif).

  • Transcript Data: Cloud storage paths to the transcript data files (e.g., .csv, .parquet).

  • Segmentation Parameters: Adjust options like tile size, model type, or thresholds.

  • Inputs

Example JSON:

{
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.algorithm": "CELLPOSE",
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.amount_of_VMs": 5,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.detected_transcripts_file": "gs://---//transcripts.parquet",
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.image_paths_list": "gs://---//image.tif",
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.technology": "XENIUM",
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.transcript_chunk_size": 100000,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.transform_file": "gs://---//transform.csv",
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.cell_prob_thresh": -1.0,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.diameter": 0,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.flow_thresh": 0.8,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.image_pixel_size": 1,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.merge_approach": "larger",
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.model_type": "",
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.optional_channel": 1,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.overlap": 400.0,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.pretrained_model": "gs://---//custom_cp2_model",
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.segment_channel": 2,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.sigma": 0,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.subset_data_y_x_interval": [1000,1500,1000,1500],
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.tiles_dimension": 3000.0,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.transcript_plot_as_channel": 0,
    "MAIN_WORKFLOW.trim_amount": 100
}
  • Running the Workflow

To execute the workflow, click Run Analysis after setting up inputs.

  • Review Outputs

After execution, outputs such as segmented cell boundaries, tiled images, assigned transcripts as well as meta data will be available in the corresponding submission ID-specific directory within the workspace-associated Cloud Storage Bucket.

docs.title: Re-training a Custom Cellpose2 Model
docs.text:
To set up Cellpose, follow the instructions provided here.

To retrain a custom Cellpose 2 model, select a few tissue regions (e.g., four) where the default segmentation results are suboptimal or inaccurate.

  • Region from the Xenium Human Skin Cancer Dataset: 246 polygons before manual curation

These selected regions will serve as training data for the custom model. Additionally, choose a separate subset of images to use as a test set.

Next, extract the default segmentation masks and refine them using the Cellpose GUI or the Celldega GUI (beta). Then, train a custom model using the Cellpose GUI by following the instructions below.

  • Upload a region of interest from your dataset into the Cellpose GUI.
  • Upload the corresponding segmentation masks and manually curate them as needed.
  • Repeat this process for different subsections of the same image to create a diverse training set.
  • Train a custom model using the curated data. Use either the GUI or the terminal (command below) to retrain the custom model:

python -m cellpose --train --dir {images_dir} --pretrained_model {base_model_name} --mask_filter _seg.npy --model_name_out {retrained_custom_model} --verbose

Once training is complete, evaluate the model using the designated test set. You may retrain the model multiple times, incorporating additional training images or adjusting model parameters as needed to improve performance.

When the model achieves satisfactory results, upload it to the appropriate Google Bucket linked to your Terra workspace. Then, reference the model in the workflow variable pretrained_model using its full bucket path.

Success criteria may include:

  • Clear qualitative improvement over default segmentation in at least one problematic tissue region
  • Increased transcript assignment rate
  • Higher total cell count
  • Greater average cell area
  • Region from the Xenium Human Skin Cancer Dataset: 312 predicted polygons by a custom Cellpose2 model after manual curation

docs.title: Jupyter Notebook Examples
docs.text: These example notebooks demonstrate how to use Celldega for spatial transcriptomics and multi-omics analysis and visualization. Each notebook is designed to be run in a Jupyter environment and showcases different features of the library.

docs.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Tutorials
docs.text:
Comprehensive tutorials that walk through complete workflows:

  • Atera Kidney Landscape-Clustergram - Direct Scanpy and AnnData steps for default clusters, linked dotplot Clustergrams, and cell-type composition across podocyte-defined glomerular gradients
  • Atera Breast Cancer Landscape-Clustergram - Loads a precomputed Scanpy clustering (or optionally recomputes it) and creates linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich widgets
  • Atera Breast Cancer Neighborhood Exploration - Continues the Atera tutorial with hextile niches linked to cell-type composition and alpha-shape overlap linked to a separate Landscape
  • Visium HD Human CRC Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich - Uses Scanpy and plain AnnData to summarize a clustered Visium HD colorectal cancer sample (signatures, fraction expressing, marker genes) and explores it in linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich widgets, ready for interactive annotation
  • Scanpy-Squidpy Xenium Pancreas - Full analysis workflow using Scanpy and Squidpy with Xenium data
  • Preprocess DegaFiles and Viz Pancreas - Preprocessing raw Xenium Pancreas data into DegaFiles and visualizing the result in a Landscape widget
  • Broad-Allen Dev Mouse Brain E15.5 Viz - Visualizes the aligned E15.5 brain as a 3D CellCloud linked to the cluster composition of every slice and to a gene-expression Clustergram

docs.title: Single Cell Tutorials
docs.text:
Tutorials that explore single-cell RNA-seq data with UMAP Landscapes linked to Clustergrams:

  • Chromium PBMC Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich - Clusters the 10x Chromium PBMC 3k dataset with Scanpy and explores it from Hugging Face: a UMAP Landscape that reads the AnnData Zarr store in the browser, a Clustergram of each cluster's rank_genes_groups markers loaded from a Matrix Zarr store, and a single-cell Clustergram of the same markers linked to its own Landscape, each with Enrich

docs.title: Brief Notebooks
docs.text:
Focused examples demonstrating specific features:

  • Landscape View Xenium - Basic Landscape visualization of Xenium data
  • Landscape from a Local Server - Viewing locally stored DegaFiles in a Landscape with dega.viz.get_local_server()
  • Atera Viz - Linked Landscape and Clustergram visualization of a Xenium breast cancer dataset
  • Atera Pre-process - Making DegaFiles from a 10x Atera output bundle with dega.pre.main and viewing them in a Landscape
  • Yearbook-Query - Using single-cell Yearbook view
  • CellCloud Thick MERFISH - 3D orbit-camera CellCloud view of thick-tissue MERFISH data
  • Landscape-Heatmap Visium-HD - Combined Landscape and heatmap visualization
  • UMAP-Cluster Pancreas Xenium - UMAP clustering with Xenium pancreas data
  • Custom Segmentation - Using custom cell segmentation with Celldega
  • Gradient Neighborhood Pancreas Islets - Building inward/outward gradient rings around pancreatic islets and profiling cell-type proportion and hormone expression with distance from the islet edge

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install Celldega and its dependencies:

pip install celldega

For full analysis workflows, you may also need:

pip install scanpy squidpy

docs.title: Embedding interactive widgets in the docs
docs.text:
The docs are rendered statically by mkdocs-jupyter, which displays saved widget state but does not execute notebooks. For an interactive Landscape / Clustergram (anywidget) to appear on the docs site, the notebook's saved widget state must be complete and its model IDs must match the cell outputs.

A plain "Run All + Save" in Jupyter Lab is unreliable for this: each Landscape streams a large message (the embedded JS bundle plus the data parquet), and the state is only captured if the widget has fully finished rendering in the browser before you save. Editing a cell and saving without a full re-execution leaves stale or missing state, and the widgets render blank.

The reliable way to (re)build a docs notebook so its widgets embed is to execute it headless with a raised iopub_timeout so those large messages aren't dropped:

jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace \
  --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=900 \
  --ExecutePreprocessor.iopub_timeout=120 \
  docs/examples/brief_notebooks/<Notebook>.ipynb

Tips:

  • Put each widget as the only expression in its own cell (separate from its construction) — anywidget embeds most reliably that way.
  • Don't add %env ANYWIDGET_HMR=1 to a docs notebook. That dev-time hot-reload watches and reloads the widget's frontend module; running it while the frontend bundle is being rebuilt can desync the saved model IDs from the cell outputs.
  • To confirm a notebook is good, check that every application/vnd.jupyter.widget-view+json model_id in the cell outputs also exists in metadata.widgets["application/vnd.jupyter.widget-state+json"].state.

docs.title: Atera Pre-process¶
docs.text:
Make DegaFiles from a 10x Atera output bundle. Atera is Xenium-class, so dega.pre.main detects an Atera bundle (by its experiment.spatial file) and runs the Xenium pipeline with Atera readers; view the result with technology="Xenium".

Requires the pre-processing extra (pip install "celldega[pre]", which needs libvips). Each region is one bundle folder, e.g. data/atera/EA_s3_broad_DX002/, containing experiment.spatial, cells.zarr.zip, transcripts.zarr.zip, cell_feature_matrix.zarr.zip, and morphology_2d/.

A large Atera WTA region (~430k cells, 3.4 billion transcripts) takes about an hour, peaks around 55 GB of memory, and produces ~20 GB of DegaFiles.

def download_repo_file(repo_id, repo_path, cache_dir, revision="main"):
    cache_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    local_path = cache_dir / Path(repo_path).name
    if local_path.exists():
        return local_path

    encoded_path = quote(repo_path)
    url = f"https://huggingface.co/datasets/{repo_id}/resolve/{revision}/{encoded_path}"
    with requests.get(url, stream=True, timeout=120) as response:
        response.raise_for_status()
        with local_path.open("wb") as handle:
            for chunk in response.iter_content(chunk_size=1024 * 1024):
                if chunk:
                    handle.write(chunk)
    return local_path

From these cell-cluster neighborhoods we can derive brand-new ones. A gradient is anchored to an existing neighborhood, so we pass the islet (endocrine) cluster's alpha shape to dega.nbhd.calc_gradient, which grows concentric rings around it and returns a new neighborhood GeoDataFrame — one ring per row, ordered inner-most to outer-most. We step every 50 µm in both directions, out to 400 µm, so the gradient reaches well into the surrounding tissue.

To stop the outward rings from overhanging into empty regions near the edges of the section, we clip them to a tissue boundary. We just hand calc_gradient the original adata via clip_reference — it extracts the cell coordinates and computes a tissue alpha shape on the fly, so the caller never has to dig out spatial arrays. clip_alpha can be coarse (a large value such as 200 µm) since we only need the overall tissue outline. The geometry is already in microns, so we leave is_pixel_space=False (the default).

Inward erosion stops automatically once a small islet erodes away, so there are fewer inward rings than outward ones.

docs.title: Gradient Neighborhoods: profiling the pancreatic islet microenvironment¶
docs.text:
This notebook demonstrates the gradient neighborhood workflow in celldega.nbhd. From a region of interest (ROI) we build concentric rings that step outward into the surrounding tissue and inward into the ROI, then measure how cell-type composition and gene expression change with distance from the ROI boundary.

Here the ROI is the set of pancreatic islets in a Xenium human pancreas section. We:

  1. Load a pre-clustered Xenium AnnData (Leiden clusters + spatial coordinates).
  2. Identify the endocrine / islet cluster from hormone markers.
  3. Define a neighborhood per cell cluster with alpha shapes, then build inward + outward gradient rings around the islet neighborhood with dega.nbhd.calc_gradient.
  4. Quantify the cell-type proportion and mean hormone expression gradient per ring.
  5. Visualize the alpha shapes and rings as static plots, a gene Clustergram, and a linked Landscape + Clustergram for interactive exploration.
  6. Optionally keep the rings and their results together in a NeighborhoodCollection.

It's a small but complete vertical slice of celldega: a dead-simple way to define neighborhoods (alpha shapes), a method to derive new ones (gradients), neighborhood-level AnnData summaries (calc_nbhd_by_pop / calc_nbhd_by_gene), and visualization (Landscape + Clustergram).

The dataset is the public Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs.h5ad and the matching DegaFiles landscape (see the Scanpy-Squidpy Xenium Pancreas tutorial for how this AnnData was produced).

docs.title: 2. Identify the islet (endocrine) cluster¶
docs.text: Pancreatic islets are marked by the endocrine hormones INS (β-cells), GCG (α-cells), SST (δ-cells), and PPY (PP-cells). We score each Leiden cluster by mean hormone expression and pick the clear winner. (In this dataset that is cluster 9 — but the score keeps the example robust if the clustering is ever re-run and the labels change.)

docs.title: 3. Define neighborhoods with alpha shapes — one per cell cluster¶
docs.text:
An alpha shape is a concave hull that wraps a point cloud. It's a refreshingly simple way to turn cells of a given type into a spatial neighborhood: no parameters to tune beyond a single length scale. dega.nbhd.alpha_shape_cell_clusters runs this for every Leiden cluster at once, and filter_alpha_shapes keeps a single value.

That length scale is inv_alpha (= 1 / alpha), and because the cell coordinates are in microns, inv_alpha is itself in microns — it's the characteristic gap the hull is allowed to bridge. A smaller value hugs the points tightly (more, smaller pieces); a larger value smooths over gaps. We use a uniform inv_alpha = 25 µm across all clusters, so each cluster becomes a MultiPolygon of its spatial domains. Keeping it small means the islets stay cleanly separated rather than getting bridged together into larger blobs.

docs.title: View all cell-cluster alpha shapes on the Landscape¶
docs.text: Passing the alpha-shape GeoDataFrame to nbhd= is all that's needed — the widget reads the micron_to_image_transform.csv from the DegaFiles base_url and converts the micron geometry to pixels itself, coloring each neighborhood by its cluster. Setting landscape_state="nbhd" reveals the neighborhood layer in the initial view (the same way landscape_state="umap" opens on the UMAP). The result is a tissue-wide map of every cell-type domain at a glance.

docs.title: Static plot — islets and their gradient rings¶
5. Quantify the gradient¶
docs.text:
Because the rings are a neighborhood GeoDataFrame, the calc_nbhd_by_* functions summarize each ring directly, returning rings × features AnnData:

  • calc_nbhd_by_pop → cell-type proportion per ring (here, the islet-cell fraction).
  • calc_nbhd_by_gene → mean expression per ring (here, the islet hormones).

Rings with fewer than 5 cells have no estimate; we reindex to every ring (filling them with 0) so the gradient axis stays complete.

docs.title: Static plots — composition and expression vs. distance from the islet edge¶
6. Clustergram of the gradient gene feature space¶
docs.text: The neighborhood-by-gene AnnData is a matrix of rings × genes, so we can cluster it as a heatmap to see which genes share a gradient profile. We keep the 40 most variable genes across the rings, transpose to genes × rings, and build a dega.clust.Matrix (row-z-scored) and a Clustergram. We set col_entity="nbhd" so the columns (rings) can link to the Landscape in the next section. Genes separate into an islet-enriched block (high inside, e.g. INS / GCG / SST) and an acinar block (high outside), while the rings order into an inward vs. outward split. (We build the Clustergram here and display it linked with the Landscape below.)

docs.title: 7. Linked Landscape + Clustergram¶
docs.text:
dega.viz.landscape_clustergram places the gradient Landscape and the Clustergram side by side and links them. Passing nbhd=gdf_grad is all the Landscape needs — it converts the micron ring geometry to pixels using the DegaFiles transform, each ring keeps its gradient color (reds inward, blues outward), and landscape_state="nbhd" shows the rings on load.

Because the clustergram's columns are the gradient rings (col_entity="nbhd") and the Landscape's neighborhood names are the same ring labels, clicking a ring column in the heatmap highlights that ring on the tissue (and toggles on the NBHD layer) — letting you read expression and spatial position together.

docs.title: 8. Optional: keep the results together in a NeighborhoodCollection¶
docs.text:
Everything above used plain objects: a GeoDataFrame of rings and the AnnData results. When you want the rings, their per-ring tables, and ring-to-ring relations kept aligned in one object (to save them together, or to subset them all at once), store them in a NeighborhoodCollection.

The collection only stores data. The celldega.nbhd functions do the computation and return plain objects, which we store with add_mod (per-ring tables) and add_relation (ring-to-ring matrices). Rings that fell below min_cells are zero-filled on the collection's ring axis.

docs.title: Cell size and continuous rotation¶
docs.text:
cell_size sets the default cell diameter in microns, assuming the centroid coordinates are in microns. Change cell_size=10.0 below and rerun the notebook to try another default.

In the interactive preview, the CELL slider multiplies this diameter: its midpoint is 1× (10 µm here), the minimum is 0×, and the maximum is 2× (20 µm here). Drag vertically or horizontally to rotate continuously, including past the poles where vertical rotation previously stopped.

The saved documentation preview uses the JavaScript bundle served by this local docs site. Reexecuting the notebook uses your locally built frontend.

docs.title: Landscape from a Local Server¶
docs.text: Celldega's widgets run in the browser and load DegaFiles (the output of dega.pre.main) over HTTP. To view DegaFiles stored on your own machine, start a local file server with dega.viz.get_local_server() and point the Landscape's base_url at it.

docs.title: Serve local DegaFiles¶
docs.text:
get_local_server() starts a background HTTP server (with CORS enabled) rooted at the notebook's working directory and returns its port. Build base_url from that port plus the path to your DegaFiles folder, relative to the working directory:

from pathlib import Path

path_dega_files = Path("data/Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs")

port = dega.viz.get_local_server()
base_url = f"http://localhost:{port}/{path_dega_files.as_posix()}"

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    technology="Xenium",
    base_url=base_url,
    height=500,
)

landscape

The server runs for the lifetime of the kernel. Run this in a live Jupyter session: the static documentation page cannot reach your localhost.

docs.title: Atera breast cancer Landscape + Clustergram + Enrich¶
docs.text:
This tutorial uses celldega>=0.26.0. It demonstrates the handoff from a precomputed Scanpy analysis plus published cell type annotations to Celldega: Scanpy provides normalized expression and UMAP coordinates, the cell types and colors come from 10x Genomics' own annotation of this dataset. Scanpy calculates expression signatures and marker rankings in plain AnnData objects; Celldega builds the all-gene hierarchy and linked interactive widgets. The first run downloads the raw 10x file and runs the Scanpy filtering, normalization, PCA, neighbors, and UMAP steps once, saving the result. Later runs load the saved AnnData and go straight to Celldega.

Data source: broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data. Downloads use a direct Hugging Face /resolve/main/ URL through Python's standard library, so huggingface_hub is not a notebook dependency. Cell types are from 10x Genomics' WTA_Preview_FFPE_Breast_Cancer_cell_groups.csv.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: If the processed AnnData is already on disk it is loaded directly. Otherwise the raw file is downloaded (if needed) and processed with Scanpy.

docs.title: Load or compute the Scanpy preprocessing¶
docs.text: Keep all genes and preserve raw counts in layers["counts"] for aggregation and detection fractions. Normalize and log-transform X for UMAP and marker testing. The saved preprocessing is also used by the neighborhood exploration tutorial; signatures and marker rankings are calculated below on each run. Cell types are added from the 10x annotation in the next section.

docs.title: 10x cell types¶
docs.text: The 10x cell groups CSV is small (one row per cell: cell_id, group, color), so it is read straight from the URL and propagated onto adata.obs by cell id. The 10x colors are stored as adata.uns["cell_type_colors"] (Scanpy's palette convention), so Scanpy, the Landscape, and the Clustergram all share them.

docs.title: Landscape¶
docs.text: Start with a full-width, 700px-high tissue view. landscape_overview is a separate widget instance from landscape, which is reserved for the linked Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich view below. Linking and resizing that view therefore leaves this overview at its original size.

docs.title: AnnData expression, fraction expressing, and marker ranks¶
docs.text: sc.get.aggregate summarizes raw counts per 10x cell type. Normalize the sums to log1p-CPM for dot colors and divide nonzero-cell counts by group size for dot sizes. Run sc.tl.rank_genes_groups directly on the log-normalized cell-level adata.X. Its standard Scanpy results are stored in signatures.uns["rank_genes_groups"]; the signatures AnnData contains all genes, their best-scoring cell type, and the same category colors as the Landscape.

docs.title: Clustergram over all genes¶
docs.text:
The full expression matrix is hierarchically clustered. Marker-ranked views are additional slider levels; they do not replace or prefilter the all-gene matrix.

Columns are colored by 10x cell type with the same palette as the Landscape. Rows are colored by a gene-level grouping derived from those cell types: each gene is assigned to the cell type where it scores highest in rank_genes_groups (signatures.var["cell_type_marker"]). Double-click a category name to reorder by it.

docs.title: Yearbook: visually query individual cells¶
docs.text:
Yearbook displays a grid of tissue portraits centered on individual cells, so you can compare their morphology and local surroundings side by side. Use its query controls to select cells by cluster or cell type, gene expression, or both. A cell-type query samples cells from that group; adding a gene ranks the matching cells by expression, highest first.

This example starts with Myeloid Cells ranked by LST1 expression. Eight portraits are shown per page, with up to 48 cells available through the paging controls. Change the cell type or gene in the Yearbook to explore another population. These queries run in the browser and also work in the saved documentation page.

docs.title: Atera breast cancer neighborhood exploration¶
docs.text:
Continue from the Atera Landscape–Clustergram tutorial. Run its data preprocessing first; this notebook reuses the saved cell list, 10x cell types and tissue coordinates. Requires celldega>=0.26.0.

Two views explore the same sample at 75 µm: cell-type composition niches from hextiles, and overlap of cell-type alpha-shape footprints. Niche labels belong to hextiles; no niche attribute is added to individual cells.

docs.title: Hextile niches¶
docs.text:
Count cell types in each tile, discard tiles with fewer than five cells, and cluster square-root proportions (Hellinger representation) with Celldega's Matrix.cluster and cut_tree. Eight niches is an exploratory resolution. The Composition bars pool cell counts across retained tiles of each niche. The broad biological names describe this 75 µm, eight-niche result; the table retains the original IDs and leading cell types so you can check them. These are composition labels, not validated histological regions. Review the names if you change the tile size or clustering resolution.

Click a column label to highlight every individual hextile of that niche. Click a row label to show that cell type across the tissue, irrespective of niche. Column dendrogram selections highlight groups of niches. The polygons remain separate hextiles, so you can also select one directly in the Landscape.

docs.title: Alpha-shape overlap¶
docs.text:
Make one footprint per cell type, retaining disconnected patches within its MultiPolygon. ALPHA_SCALE_UM is the inverse-alpha shape scale in microns, not a tile diameter. Empty footprints are omitted.

Calculate intersection areas with dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_overlap, then column-normalize with Matrix.norm: each column sums to one, including self-overlap on the diagonal. A value is a share of the column's summed intersection areas, not the fraction of its unique area covered by a cell type; overlapping footprints can count the same area more than once.

Click any matrix tile, including a zero, to highlight both footprints and inspect their spatial overlap or separation. Row/column labels select one footprint; dendrogram selections highlight groups with similar overlap profiles. These footprints describe spatial mixing of cell types, not cell–cell contacts.

docs.title: Atera kidney: default clusters and glomerular gradients¶
docs.text:
Compare the dataset's 28 default Leiden clusters in a linked Landscape–dotplot Clustergram, then measure how cell-type composition changes with distance from podocyte-defined glomerular footprints.

Watch on YouTube

Default cluster 16 contains 5,172 cells, 96.7% with a supplied Podocyte annotation. We use its spatial nodules as candidate glomeruli, then summarize the supplied Azimuth coarse cell types inside and around them. The gradient uses all 399,120 cell centroids, including cells without a default cluster.

The workflow uses AnnData, GeoDataFrames, Scanpy, and the neighborhood module's geometry functions. There are no collection classes, inline helper functions, signature caches, or sub-clustering steps. Manual category tracks are disabled in the linked default-cluster view.

The data are the public Atera WTA FFPE human non-diseased kidney dataset from 10x Genomics, with over 1 billion transcripts. Use the dega environment on the atera_preprocess branch. DegaFiles are on GitHub; annotated raw counts are on Hugging Face. The count file is 1.31 GiB; allow several GiB of memory.

docs.title: Cell-type context for the default clusters¶
docs.text:
The supplied Azimuth coarse labels provide a guide to a few default clusters:

Default cluster(s) Main supplied cell-type annotation 2 B cells (76.9%) 11 Macrophages (77.9%) 15 T cells (65.9%) 16 Podocytes (96.7%), used for glomerular footprints below 21, 22, 24 Proximal-tubule epithelial cells (95–100%) 13 Endothelial cells (94.6%)

These annotations describe cluster composition; they do not rename or independently validate the default clusters.

docs.title: Wide Landscape overview¶
docs.text: Explore the full tissue and its original default clusters. This full-width Landscape is a separate widget from the linked views below, so their selections and resizing leave this overview independent.

docs.title: Look up cells with Yearbook¶
docs.text: Yearbook shows a grid of portraits centered on individual cells, using the same default clusters as the Landscape above. Query by cluster, gene, or both: a cluster query samples its cells, and adding a gene ranks them by expression, highest first. This example starts with cluster 16 (podocytes) ranked by NPHS2. Change the cluster or gene in the Yearbook controls to look up other cells.

docs.title: Default cluster signatures¶
docs.text:
All 28 default clusters pass the 100-cell minimum: 398,873 labeled cells; 247 unlabeled cells are excluded from the linked views. cells.X contains raw counts, and its original Leiden colors match the DegaFiles.

First aggregate counts and detection fractions into a clusters × genes AnnData. Dot colors will show log1p CPM, z-scored per gene; dot sizes will show the fraction of cells expressing each gene.

docs.title: Linked default-cluster view¶
docs.text: Pass the signatures AnnData to Matrix, and a second AnnData with detection fractions to set_size_matrix. Click a gene row to show spatial expression, or a cluster column to select its cells. The DIM slider changes the number of top markers per cluster; all 18,049 genes remain available.

docs.title: Podocyte-defined glomerular footprints¶
docs.text:
Use dega.nbhd.alpha_shape on cluster 16 at an inverse-alpha scale of 40 µm. Fill enclosed holes so the footprint includes the nodule interior, union any nested components, and retain components supported by at least 10 podocytes. These are candidate footprints, not histologically segmented glomeruli; the scale and support cutoff are exploratory settings.

At these settings, 119 footprints contain 4,430 of the 5,172 seed cells. The other seed cells do not define a retained footprint, but remain eligible for the composition counts.

SEED_CLUSTERS is a list so you can add other default clusters. Start with ["16"]: including a broadly distributed endothelial or stromal cluster without a spatial restriction can connect unrelated regions.

docs.title: Distance bands in a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text:
dega.nbhd.calc_gradient returns 25 µm bands, measured from the footprint boundary: negative distances are inside, positive distances are outside, up to 200 µm. It unions the footprints before buffering, so neighboring glomeruli do not double-count the same surrounding tissue. Outward bands are clipped to a tissue alpha shape built from all cell centroids (inverse alpha 200 µm).

The resulting rings is a plain GeoDataFrame. The spatial check below shows the whole section and a zoom near its center. Black outlines delimit footprints; red bands lie inside and blue bands outside.

docs.title: Count cell types with a spatial join¶
docs.text:
Count each cell once, even on shared band boundaries: intersects includes hull vertices, and ties go to the more inward band. This matters because many seed podocytes are exactly on their footprint's boundary.

Use the supplied coarse annotations, keeping uncertain and unassigned cells in the denominator. No minimum cell-type size is imposed on the analysis. population is an AnnData with bands × cell types: proportions in X, integer counts in layers["counts"], and distances and sample sizes in obs. Cell-to-band assignments remain in spatial_cells.obs["glomerulus_band"]; cells outside the analyzed region have missing assignments.

docs.title: Cell-type composition versus distance¶
docs.text:
For display only, retain cell types reaching 2% in any band and combine the remaining types into Other. All individual categories remain in population. The upper panel shows the number of cells supporting each estimate; the lower panel shows proportions. Zero marks the footprint boundary.

These are pooled, cell-weighted proportions from one section, not averages over glomeruli or biological replicates. Deep inward bands sample only the larger footprints. Podocyte enrichment at the boundary is partly built into how the footprints were defined.

docs.title: Linked Landscape–Composition view¶
docs.text:
Composition accepts an AnnData directly. Set col_entity="nbhd" so its distance-band columns select the matching GeoDataFrame geometries in a separate Landscape. The row entity names the cell-type attribute shared with that Landscape; clicking a stacked segment highlights its cell type and distance band together.

cluster=False preserves distance order. The distance and cell-count tracks expose each band's metadata, and the PROP/COUNTS toggle compares proportions with cell counts. Cell colors match the static plot, including the display-only Other group. The complete, uncollapsed analysis remains in population. The wide overview and default-cluster view above stay independent.

docs.title: Reading this run¶
docs.text:
There are 149,833 unique cells across 11 bands (three inward and eight outward), with 52 supplied coarse labels represented. The deepest band contains 286 cells; the other bands contain 2,928–19,631 cells.

Within 0–25 µm outside the footprints, endothelial-labeled cells account for 16.3%, proximal-tubule-labeled cells 3.9%, and macrophages 7.0%. At 175–200 µm outside, those proportions are 8.3%, 21.1%, and 8.0%, respectively. Endothelial labels reach 44.1% in the deepest inward band. These changes describe the supplied annotations in this section; inspect the footprints and label confidence before interpreting them biologically.

The source counts, labels, and DegaFiles are unchanged. The following exports contain the full composition table, candidate footprints, distance bands, and an expression-free AnnData with cell coordinates and band assignments. They can be joined to the original expression AnnData by cell ID.

docs.title: Broad-Allen Developing Mouse Brain E15.5: Viz¶
docs.text:
This tutorial uses celldega>=0.28. It visualizes a 3D alignment of the serial sections (made with the separate dega-collection package and written to DegaFiles with dega.pre.write_point_cloud_dataset):

  1. Visualize in 2D: a Landscape of one slice at full resolution.
  2. Explore the clusters in 3D: a wide Composition plot of the Leiden clusters in every slice introduces the clusters along the front-to-back axis. A CellCloud of all 3.8 million aligned cells, linked to a Clustergram of the 480-gene signatures of the clusters, then lets you explore them.

Using the linked widgets. Drag to orbit around the brain and scroll to zoom. Click a column of the Clustergram (a cluster) to highlight that cluster in 3D, or a row (a gene) to color the cells by its expression.

Watch on YouTube

docs.title: The experiment¶
docs.text:
This dataset is being generated in collaboration with the Allen Institute. It is whole-brain spatial transcriptomics of a mouse embryo at E15.5. The brain was cut into 44 coronal sections, ordered from the front of the brain (slice 1, anterior) to the back (slice 44, posterior), with a section taken every 100 µm, and profiled with the 10x Xenium platform and a 480-gene panel. Cells were segmented from the images, which gives each cell a position (in µm) and a gene-count vector. After quality control the dataset holds about 3.8 million cells.

All cells from all slices were clustered together with Leiden using rapids-singlecell on Manifold.ai, so a cluster means the same thing in every slice. The clustered AnnData (raw counts, cell positions, slice numbers and Leiden labels) is hosted on Hugging Face: Allen-Broad_Dev-Mouse-Brain/E15.5/xenium_E15.5_clustered.h5ad (about 1.9 GB).

The DegaFiles (the 3D CellCloud and the 2D Landscape of slice 35) are hosted on GitHub at broadinstitute/celldega_xenium_E15.5_cell_cloud.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: The widgets read their DegaFiles straight from GitHub. The clustered AnnData, used for the composition and the gene signatures, is downloaded from Hugging Face unless it is already on disk.

docs.title: 1. Visualize in 2D: a Landscape of one slice¶
docs.text:
A Landscape shows one slice at full resolution: the DAPI and cell-boundary images, the cell outlines, and the transcripts of every gene. Cells are colored by their Leiden cluster, and the UMAP of the slice's cells is available from the control panel. Here we show slice 35, in the posterior part of the brain.

The cells in the AnnData are named <slice>_<cell id>. cell_name_prefix=True drops the slice prefix so the names match the cell ids of the slice's Xenium output.

docs.title: Cluster composition across slices¶
docs.text: The composition plot shows, for every slice (one bar each, anterior to posterior), the share of cells in each Leiden cluster. It gives an overview of all clusters at once and shows which ones belong to which part of the brain along the front-to-back axis.

docs.title: Gene-expression signatures of the clusters¶
docs.text:
Matrix(adata, groupby=...) summarizes each Leiden cluster with scanpy: the mean log-normalized expression (sc.get.aggregate), the fraction of the cluster's cells expressing each gene, and the top marker genes of each cluster (sc.tl.rank_genes_groups).

Marker ranking works on log-normalized expression of every cell, which for 3.8 million cells needs far more memory than a laptop has. The signatures are therefore computed from a random sample of up to 20,000 cells per cluster (all cells of smaller clusters). For this dataset the sampled signatures correlate with those of all cells at r > 0.999 for every cluster.

docs.title: Linked 3D view¶
docs.text:
A CellCloud of every aligned cell, linked to the Clustergram. Click a column of the Clustergram to highlight that cluster in 3D, or a row to color the cells by that gene's expression.

The CellCloud holds both alignments of the same cells. Pass alignment="centroids" to see the result of step 1 alone.

docs.title: Preprocess DegaFiles and Viz — Pancreas¶
docs.text:
A minimal end-to-end walkthrough of the Celldega pipeline on the public Xenium V1 Human Pancreas (FFPE) dataset: download the raw data (only if it isn't already present), run dega.pre.main to generate DegaFiles, then view the result in a Landscape widget.

Data source: https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/ffpe-human-pancreas-with-xenium-multimodal-cell-segmentation-1-standard

docs.title: 1. Download raw Xenium data (only if needed)¶
docs.text: Checks for the extracted data first, then the downloaded archive, and only curls / unzips what's missing — so re-running the notebook doesn't re-download ~9 GB every time.

docs.title: 2. Run preprocessing → DegaFiles¶
docs.text: dega.pre.main reads the raw Xenium output under data_root_dir/sample and writes the DegaFiles landscape bundle to path_dega_files.

docs.title: 3. Visualize the DegaFiles in a Landscape¶
docs.text: By default this renders the Landscape widget from a public GitHub-hosted copy of these same Pancreas DegaFiles, so the cell below works immediately — without waiting on steps 1–2 to download/preprocess anything.

docs.title: Using your own locally generated DegaFiles instead¶
docs.text:
To view the files you generated in step 2 (path_dega_files) rather than the GitHub-hosted copy, serve them from a local server and point base_url there instead of the URL above:

server_address = dega.viz.get_local_server()
base_url = f"http://localhost:{server_address}/{path_dega_files}"

landscape_ist = dega.viz.Landscape(
    technology="Xenium",
    base_url=base_url,
)

landscape_ist

docs.title: Chromium PBMC 3k: Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich¶
docs.text:
Cluster the 10x Genomics Chromium PBMC 3k dataset with Scanpy, save the AnnData to Zarr, and explore it with Celldega:

  • Landscape reads the cells, clusters, UMAP, and per-gene expression straight from the AnnData Zarr store in the browser, with no DegaFiles. Color cells by a gene, or plot two genes against each other in the XY view.
  • Clustergram shows each cluster's rank_genes_groups markers, clustered hierarchically with Matrix and saved to Zarr too.
  • A single-cell Clustergram shows the same markers in every cell, so you can see how they vary within each cluster.
  • Enrich finds gene sets enriched in a Clustergram selection.

Like a baking show, the recipe comes first and the finished result comes out of the oven: the steps below were already run, and the notebook loads their output from Hugging Face.

This notebook needs Celldega 0.28 or later (pip install --pre celldega until 0.28.0 is released), zarr>=3, and anndata>=0.12,<0.13. The stores use Zarr format 3: an older Zarr 2 environment can report PathNotFoundError even when the URL is valid.

docs.title: The recipe: cluster with Scanpy¶
docs.text:
The standard Scanpy workflow on the 10x PBMC 3k dataset. The raw counts are kept in a layer: Landscape shows them, the same values DegaFiles store.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import scanpy as sc
import zarr

data_dir = Path("data/pbmc3k")
sc.settings.datasetdir = data_dir
adata = sc.datasets.pbmc3k()
adata.var_names_make_unique()

sc.pp.filter_cells(adata, min_genes=200)
sc.pp.filter_genes(adata, min_cells=3)
adata.var["mt"] = adata.var_names.str.startswith("MT-")
sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics(adata, qc_vars=["mt"], percent_top=None, log1p=False, inplace=True)
adata = adata[(adata.obs["n_genes_by_counts"] < 2500) & (adata.obs["pct_counts_mt"] < 5)].copy()

adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(adata, n_top_genes=2000)
sc.tl.pca(adata, mask_var="highly_variable", random_state=0)
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_neighbors=10, n_pcs=40, random_state=0)
sc.tl.umap(adata, random_state=0)
sc.tl.leiden(adata, flavor="igraph", directed=False, n_iterations=2, resolution=0.9, random_state=0)
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(adata, groupby="leiden", method="wilcoxon", use_raw=False)
# Stores the cluster colors in adata.uns["leiden_colors"].
sc.pl.umap(adata, color="leiden", legend_loc="on data")

docs.title: The recipe: save the AnnData to Zarr for Landscape¶
docs.text:
Landscape reads one gene at a time from a column-compressed (CSC) copy of the counts: each gene's values are contiguous, so the browser fetches only that gene. The per-gene mean and max, used to rank the gene bars and scale cell colors, go in var. Consolidated metadata lets the browser open the store in one request.

adata.layers["counts_csc"] = adata.layers["counts"].tocsc()
adata.var["mean"] = np.asarray(adata.layers["counts_csc"].mean(axis=0)).ravel()
adata.var["max"] = adata.layers["counts_csc"].max(axis=0).toarray().ravel()

# Write every chunk, even all-zero ones: Hugging Face answers 403 rather than
# 404 for a missing file.
with zarr.config.set({"array.write_empty_chunks": True}):
    adata.write_zarr(data_dir / "pbmc3k.zarr")
zarr.consolidate_metadata(data_dir / "pbmc3k.zarr")

docs.title: The recipe: cluster the markers with Matrix¶
docs.text:
Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden") aggregates the cells of every gene into a dot plot (mean expression as color, the fraction of expressing cells as size) and reuses the rank_genes_groups markers. cluster(view="rank_genes_groups") adds a slider for the top markers per cluster, with the full transcriptome as its "all" stop. write_zarr saves the clustered result.

import celldega as dega

mat = dega.clust.Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden", col_attr=["leiden"], name="pbmc3k_leiden")
mat.norm("row", by="zscore")
mat.cluster(view="rank_genes_groups", levels=[1, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 200])
mat.write_zarr(data_dir / "pbmc3k_leiden_markers.zarr")

Both stores were then uploaded to a Hugging Face dataset:

hf upload broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data data/pbmc3k/pbmc3k.zarr pbmc3k/pbmc3k.zarr --repo-type dataset
hf upload broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data data/pbmc3k/pbmc3k_leiden_markers.zarr pbmc3k/pbmc3k_leiden_markers.zarr --repo-type dataset

docs.title: Out of the oven: explore from Hugging Face¶
docs.text:
zarr_url points the Landscape at the AnnData Zarr store. Python only passes the URL along: the browser reads the store's metadata, clusters, colors, and UMAP, and then fetches each gene's values when you select it, the same way it reads DegaFiles. So the Landscape also works in a saved, kernel-free notebook. Matrix.read_zarr loads the clustered markers without re-clustering.

Click a cluster or a gene to color the UMAP. To plot two genes against each other, select them (shift-click the gene bars) and click XY, or click XY and type them in the autocompleting X and Y inputs. Select Clustergram rows to run Enrich, and click a gene in Enrich to color the cells by it.

docs.title: Single-cell Clustergram¶
docs.text:
The Clustergram above summarizes each cluster as one column. To see how the markers vary from cell to cell, load the AnnData itself (about 25 MB from Hugging Face) and build a Matrix with genes as rows and individual cells as columns, colored by their Leiden cluster. The values are the log-normalized expression in adata.X, z-scored across cells for each gene. col_entity="cell" marks the columns as individual cells, so Clustergram selections highlight those cells in a linked Landscape.

The AnnData carries Scanpy's rank_genes_groups results, so cluster(view="rank_genes_groups") adds the same RANK slider for the top markers per cluster. The rows are each cluster's top 50 markers, the slider's "all" stop, which keeps the matrix small enough to cluster and display.

docs.title: Selected cells¶
docs.text:
With a running kernel, get_selected_cells() returns the IDs of the selected cells: a cluster, a Clustergram dendrogram selection, or the cells inside a drawn gate. Pass the AnnData loaded above to subset it to those cells:

selected = landscape.get_selected_cells(adata)

docs.title: Visium HD human colorectal cancer Landscape + Clustergram + Enrich¶
docs.text:
This tutorial explores a Visium HD human colorectal cancer (CRC) sample that was already segmented into cells and clustered with Scanpy (220,703 cells, 15 Leiden clusters). It shows the handoff from Scanpy to Celldega:

  1. view the clustered cells in their tissue context with a Landscape,
  2. summarize clusters in a plain AnnData: pseudobulk expression, the fraction of cells expressing each gene, and marker genes ranked per cluster,
  3. explore the result in a Clustergram linked to the Landscape and to Enrich (Enrichr gene-set enrichment),
  4. annotate clusters and genes interactively, and
  5. sub-cluster the Goblet cells and color the sub-clusters by their depth along the colonic crypts.

Watch on YouTube

Data source: broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data. Files are downloaded once through direct Hugging Face /resolve/main/ URLs, so huggingface_hub is not a notebook dependency.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text:
Two files are used, each downloaded on first run and reused afterwards:

  • crc_cluster.h5ad (~1.6 GB): the Scanpy analysis, with log-normalized expression in X, Leiden clusters in obs["leiden"], and a UMAP.
  • crc_raw_feature_cell_matrix.h5 (~280 MB): Space Ranger's cell-segmented count matrix for the same sample, which supplies the raw counts the analysis file does not keep.

docs.title: Wide Landscape overview¶
docs.text: The Landscape loads pre-tiled image and segmentation data (LandscapeFiles) from base_url and takes cell metadata, including the Leiden clusters, from adata. This full-width overview is a separate widget from the linked views below, so their selections leave it unchanged.

docs.title: Look up cells with Yearbook¶
docs.text: Yearbook shows a grid of portraits centered on individual cells, using the same Leiden clusters as the Landscape above. Query by cluster, gene, or both: a cluster query samples its cells, and adding a gene ranks them by expression, highest first. This example starts with cluster 4 (Goblet cells) ranked by MUC2. Change the cluster or gene in the Yearbook controls to look up other cells.

docs.title: Landscape¶
docs.text: A second Landscape, linked below to the Clustergram and Enrich, with the full adata (including its UMAP).

docs.title: AnnData cluster signatures and marker genes¶
docs.text: Aggregate raw counts with sc.get.aggregate. The resulting AnnData holds log1p-CPM pseudobulk expression in X, detection fractions in layers["fraction_expressing"], and the shared cluster palette in obs["color"]. Run sc.tl.rank_genes_groups on cell-level log-normalized adata.X and copy its results into signatures.uns["rank_genes_groups"]. Each gene's best-scoring cluster colors its row.

docs.title: Clustergram¶
docs.text: The Matrix colors columns by cluster (col_attr=["leiden"]) and rows by each gene's best-scoring cluster (row_attr=["leiden_marker"]), using the same palette as the Landscape. All genes are hierarchically clustered; the marker-ranked views add DIM slider levels with each cluster's top 1, 2, 3, ... markers, each re-biclustered ahead of time. rank_dim=3 opens on the top 3 markers per cluster.

docs.title: Linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich¶
docs.text:
• Click a column (cluster) label to highlight that cluster in the Landscape and send its top marker genes to Enrich.
  • Click a gene (row) label to show that gene's expression in the Landscape.
  • Select a dendrogram cluster of genes to run enrichment on that gene set.
  • Drag the DIM slider to move between marker-ranked views and all genes.
  • Use the ROW / COL dropdowns in the control panel to switch which category the bar plots summarize, and hover a category to locate it in the matrix.
  • Annotate: select columns or rows (e.g. from a dendrogram) and assign a cell_type or info category. Annotations are colored in the matrix and summarized in the category bars.

docs.title: Sub-clustering Goblet cells along the crypt axis¶
docs.text:
Leiden cluster 4 (Goblet / mucin-secreting epithelial cells, 15,613 cells) lines the colonic crypts. Re-clustering these cells reveals epithelial states that may vary along the crypt axis. The ordering below is a working interpretation to check against tissue position and the full expression signatures.

The sub-clusters were calculated from cluster 4's raw counts:

goblet = sc.AnnData(adata[adata.obs["leiden"] == "4"].layers["counts"].copy())
sc.pp.normalize_total(goblet)
sc.pp.log1p(goblet)
sc.tl.pca(goblet)
sc.pp.neighbors(goblet, n_neighbors=30, metric="correlation")
sc.tl.leiden(goblet, flavor="igraph", resolution=1.0, random_state=0)
sc.tl.umap(goblet, min_dist=0.5, spread=2, random_state=0)
# Sub-clusters are then relabeled 0, 1, 2, ... from largest to smallest.

Here the precomputed result is downloaded instead. It has the same cell barcodes as adata, log-normalized expression in X, sub-clusters in obs["leiden"], and a sub-cluster UMAP.

Sub-clusters 3 and 6 remain excluded from this working selection. They retain Goblet-marker expression, so this exclusion needs review and is not a validated cell-type annotation. The remaining nine sub-clusters keep their original Leiden labels and UMAP coordinates.

docs.title: A speculative crypt orientation¶
docs.text: The sub-clusters are given a working order from the crypt base to the surface (CRYPT_ORDER below). This orientation is speculative: check it against tissue position and the full signatures in the Clustergram. crypt_depth is an ordinal label (9 at the proposed base to 1 at the surface), not a measured distance, and the colors are a display gradient. Sub-clusters 7 and 9 occupy separate crypts, so their positions on the axis are uncertain.

docs.title: Sub-cluster signatures and marker genes¶
docs.text:
The sub-clusters are summarized in an AnnData, the same way as the clusters above. Raw counts come from the main adata, which has the same cells and genes. This Clustergram retains the full gene space: use its DIM slider (0 = all genes) to explore it.

Each sub-cluster's crypt_depth is added as a numeric column attribute. Double-click its label in the Clustergram to order the sub-clusters from the crypt base (left) to the surface (right).

Genes get the same attribute: after the marker ranking, each gene takes the depth of its best-scoring sub-cluster (var["leiden_marker"]). Double-click the row attribute label to order marker genes from the crypt base (top) to the surface (bottom). Genes without a marker score have depth 0.

docs.title: Goblet sub-clusters in the tissue¶
docs.text: Only the retained cells are colored in this Landscape. Under the proposed orientation, purple indicates the crypt base and yellow the surface; the green crypts in the upper region are sub-clusters 7 and 9. Click a sub-cluster column in the Clustergram to highlight its cells in the tissue and send its top marker genes to Enrich. In the Landscape, switch to the UMAP view to see the sub-cluster embedding.

JavaScript API Overview
docs.text: Celldega's visualization methods can be used as a stand-alone JavaScript library outside the context of a Jupyter notebook. This enables creating showcase visualizations with publicly hosted data, embedding visualizations in web applications, and building custom interactive experiences.

docs.title: Using in HTML
docs.text:
You can include Celldega in any HTML page by importing the bundled JavaScript module:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <style>
        #landscape-container {
            width: 100%;
            height: 800px;
            border: 1px solid #ccc;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <div id="landscape-container"></div>

    <script type="module">
        import celldega from './celldega.js';

        document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", async () => {
            const el = document.getElementById('landscape-container');

            const landscape = await celldega.landscape_ist(
                el,                    // DOM element
                {},                    // model (empty for standalone)
                '',                    // token
                10000,                 // initial X
                10000,                 // initial Y
                0,                     // initial Z
                -5,                    // initial zoom
                'https://your-data-url/LandscapeFiles',  // base URL
                'Dataset Name',        // dataset name
                0.25,                  // transcript radius
                '100%',                // width
                '100%'                 // height
            );
        });
    </script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Using with ObservableHQ
docs.text: Celldega can be used in ObservableHQ notebooks. See the Celldega Landscape Xenium example for a working demo.

docs.title: Available Functions
docs.text:
Celldega exports the following main visualization functions:

Function Description landscape_ist Create an interactive spatial transcriptomics (IST) landscape visualization landscape_h_e Create an H&E image visualization matrix_viz Create a Clustergrammer-style matrix/heatmap visualization yearbook Create a yearbook-style grid of cell portraits

docs.title: Data Requirements
docs.text:
For standalone JavaScript visualizations, your data must be hosted publicly (e.g., on GitHub, S3, or a web server). The data should be in the LandscapeFiles format, which includes:

  • landscape_parameters.json - Configuration file
  • pyramid_images/ - Image tile pyramids
  • cell_metadata.parquet - Cell positions
  • cell_segmentation/ - Cell boundary tiles
  • trx_tiles/ - Transcript location tiles
  • meta_gene.parquet - Gene metadata

See the File Formats documentation for details.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: For detailed API documentation of each function, see the API Reference.

docs.title: Celldega JavaScript API Documentation
docs.text: The JavaScript component of Celldega is used within the Jupyter Widgets framework to provide interactive visualization in the context of a Jupyter notebook but can also be used as a standalone JavaScript library.

docs.title: Visualizations without Python: landscape, clustergram, and link_models
docs.text: landscape and clustergram render Celldega visualizations in a plain web page, without a Python kernel, from data on any static file server that allows cross-origin requests (a local server, a bucket, or Hugging Face). Each takes the container element and an options object, and returns the visualization with its model and a finalize() method. The lower-level landscape_ist and matrix_viz renderers, documented below, remain available.

docs.title: landscape(el, options)
docs.text:
The options are the Python Landscape's arguments, with the same defaults, for example:

  • zarr_url (string): a single-cell AnnData Zarr store (see Landscape(zarr_url=...)), or
  • base_url (string): DegaFiles;
  • cluster_attr (string, 'leiden' by default) and cell_attr (string[]): the cell attributes to show, with cluster_attr coloring the cells;
  • technology ('Chromium' by default with zarr_url, otherwise 'Xenium'), ini_x, ini_y, ini_zoom, height, width, dataset_name, and the Landscape's other arguments.

Passing both zarr_url and base_url is an error.

docs.title: clustergram(el, options)
docs.text:
Pass exactly one data source:

  • network (object): a Clustergram network object, like a Clustergrammer network JSON;
  • url (string): a clustered Matrix saved with Matrix.write_zarr, which Matrix.read_zarr also loads in Python; or
  • base_url (string) and name (string, 'default' by default): a Clustergram in DegaFiles.

The other options are width and height (500 by default), viz_mode ('heatmap' or 'dotplot', the latter by default when the data has a size matrix), rank_dim (see matrix_from_zarr), the row_label_callback, col_label_callback, and col_dendro_callback click callbacks, and fetchOptions for every request.

docs.title: link_models(source, source_key, target, target_key)
docs.text: Copies one visualization's model value to another whenever it changes, like ipywidgets' jslink in one direction, and returns a function that removes the link. Linking a Clustergram's click_info to a Landscape's update_trigger does what spatial_clustergram does in Python: clicking a gene colors the cells by it, and clicking a cluster selects its cells.

docs.title: Example: a single-cell Landscape and Clustergram from Hugging Face
docs.text:
import celldega from 'celldega';

const HF_URL =
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data/resolve/main/pbmc3k';

const landscape = await celldega.landscape(document.getElementById('landscape'), {
    zarr_url: `${HF_URL}/pbmc3k.zarr`,
    cluster_attr: 'leiden',
    ini_zoom: -4.5,
    ini_x: 5000,
    ini_y: 5000,
});
const clustergram = await celldega.clustergram(document.getElementById('matrix'), {
    url: `${HF_URL}/pbmc3k_leiden_markers.zarr`,
    rank_dim: 10,
});
celldega.link_models(clustergram.model, 'click_info', landscape.model, 'update_trigger');

The repository's celldega_js_examples/single_cell_from_zarr.html and clustergram_from_zarr.html are complete pages.

docs.title: Data readers
docs.text:
• network_from_zarr(url) returns the network object of a clustered Matrix Zarr store, and network_from_dega_files(base_url, name) (also available as networkFromDegaFiles) that of a DegaFiles Clustergram.
  • anndata_zarr_source(url, options) opens a single-cell AnnData Zarr store for a Landscape: its cells, genes, metadata, and a reader that fetches one gene at a time.

docs.title: landscape_ist API Documentation
docs.text: The landscape_ist function initializes and renders an interactive spatial transcriptomics (IST) landscape visualization. This API is designed to work with Deck.gl and includes customizable visualization options, dynamic data updates, and UI interactions.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• el (HTMLElement): The root DOM element where the visualization is rendered.
  • ini_model (Object): The initial data model containing configuration and state.
  • token (string): Authentication token for accessing data.
  • ini_x, ini_y, ini_z (number): Initial spatial coordinates for the view.
  • ini_zoom (number): Initial zoom level for the visualization.
  • base_url (string): Base URL for accessing data files.
  • dataset_name (string, optional): Name of the dataset being visualized.
  • trx_radius (number, optional): Initial radius for transcript points. Default: 0.25.
  • width (number|string, optional): Width of the visualization. Default: 100%.
  • height (number, optional): Height of the visualization. Default: 800.
  • view_change_custom_callback (Function, optional): Custom callback triggered on view changes.

docs.title: Public API
docs.text: The landscape_ist function returns an object (landscape) with several methods for interacting with the visualization.

docs.title: update_matrix_gene
docs.text: Updates the visualization to highlight data for a specific gene.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • inst_gene (string): The gene to highlight.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Updates the transcript layer to show data for the specified gene.
  • Scrolls the bar graph to bring the selected gene into view.
  • Toggles visibility of image layers and controls based on the selected gene.

docs.title: update_matrix_col
docs.text: Updates the visualization to highlight data for a specific column (e.g., cluster).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • inst_col (string): The column to highlight.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Highlights the bar graph corresponding to the selected column.
  • Updates cell and path layers to reflect the selected column.
  • Toggles visibility of layers based on the column selection.

docs.title: update_matrix_dendro_col
docs.text: Updates the visualization based on a dendrogram selection of columns.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • selected_cols (Array<string>): The list of selected column names.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Highlights the selected columns in the bar graph.
  • Updates layers to reflect the selection.

docs.title: update_view_state
docs.text: Updates the view state of the Deck.gl visualization.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• new_view_state (Object): The new view state configuration.
  • close_up (boolean): Whether the view should zoom in closely.
  • trx_layer (Object): The transcript layer to update.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: • Adjusts the viewport and reconfigures layers based on the new view state.

docs.title: update_layers
docs.text: Updates all visualization layers.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: • Refreshes the Deck.gl layers with the current visualization state.

docs.title: finalize
docs.text: Finalizes the Deck.gl instance and cleans up resources.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: • Disposes of all Deck.gl resources and event listeners to prevent memory leaks.

docs.title: Usage Example
docs.text:
javascript
import { landscape_ist } from 'path/to/landscape_ist';

const rootElement = document.getElementById('visualization-container');
const model = { /* Model containing visualization data */ };

const visualization = await landscape_ist(
    rootElement,
    model,
    'example-token',
    100,
    200,
    0,
    -5,
    'https://example.com/data',
    'Example Dataset'
);

// Update the visualization with a specific gene.
visualization.update_matrix_gene('TP53');

// Update the visualization with a specific column.
visualization.update_matrix_col('Cluster 1');

// Finalize the visualization when done.
visualization.finalize();

docs.title: matrix_viz API Documentation
docs.text: The matrix_viz function initializes and renders a matrix visualization. This API is built using approaches and code adaptations from the Clustergrammer-GL library, and it integrates tightly with Deck.gl to provide interactive and dynamic visualizations.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• model (Object): The model object containing configuration data for the visualization.
  • el (HTMLElement): The root DOM element where the visualization is rendered.
  • network (Object): The network object containing the matrix data to visualize.
  • width (string|number, optional): The width of the visualization. Default: '800'.
  • height (string|number, optional): The height of the visualization. Default: '800'.
  • row_label_callback (Function, optional): A callback function triggered on row label interactions.
  • col_label_callback (Function, optional): A callback function triggered on column label interactions.
  • col_dendro_callback (Function, optional): A callback function triggered on dendrogram column interactions.

docs.title: Internal Behavior
docs.text:
The function performs the following setup: 1. Deck.gl Integration: - Initializes a Deck.gl instance for the matrix visualization. - Sets properties for interactivity, including tooltips, view state changes, and layer filtering.

  1. Matrix Data Setup:
  2. Parses and structures the matrix data from the network object.

  3. Configures labels, categories, and dendrograms for both rows and columns.

  4. Layer Initialization:

  5. Creates layers for:
    • Matrix cells.
    • Row and column labels.
    • Row and column categories.
    • Row and column dendrograms.

  6. Attaches interactions (e.g., click events) to these layers.

  7. UI Setup:

  8. Creates a container for the visualization and appends it to the root DOM element.

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
import { matrix_viz } from 'path/to/matrix_viz';

const rootElement = document.getElementById('matrix-container');
const model = { /* Model containing visualization data */ };
const network = { /* Network object representing the matrix data */ };

// Callback functions
const rowLabelCallback = (row) => {
    console.log('Row label clicked:', row);
};

const colLabelCallback = (col) => {
    console.log('Column label clicked:', col);
};

const colDendroCallback = (dendro) => {
    console.log('Column dendrogram clicked:', dendro);
};

// Initialize the matrix visualization
await matrix_viz(
    model,
    rootElement,
    network,
    800,
    800,
    rowLabelCallback,
    colLabelCallback,
    colDendroCallback
);

docs.title: matrix_from_zarr API Documentation (experimental)
docs.text: matrix_from_zarr renders a Clustergram from a clustered Matrix saved in Python with Matrix.write_zarr, without a Python kernel. It is the same as clustergram(el, {url, ...}). It reads the AnnData Zarr store with zarrita, so the store can be hosted on any static file server that allows cross-origin requests.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• el (HTMLElement): The container element.
  • options (object):
  • url (string): URL of the .zarr store.
  • width, height (number, optional): Size of the matrix, 500 by default.
  • viz_mode (string, optional): 'heatmap' or 'dotplot'; defaults to 'dotplot' when the store has a size matrix.
  • rank_dim (number, optional): Opens at this precomputed view level, for example 10 for the top 10 markers per cluster of cluster(view="rank_genes_groups"), like Python's Clustergram(rank_dim=...). Opens the full matrix by default.
  • row_label_callback, col_label_callback, col_dendro_callback (function, optional): Called on row label, column label, and column dendrogram clicks.
  • fetchOptions (object, optional): Options passed to every fetch, for example authentication headers.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import celldega from 'celldega';

const el = document.getElementById('clustergram');
await celldega.matrix_from_zarr(el, {
    url: 'https://example.org/pbmc_markers.zarr',
    width: 600,
    height: 600,
});

network_from_zarr(url) returns the same store's network object, for passing to matrix_viz directly.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Celldega is a spatial analysis and visualization library developed by the Spatial Technology Platform at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. It enables researchers to easily visualize and analyze large spatial transcriptomics (ST) datasets (e.g., datasets with >100M transcripts) alongside single-cell and spatial analysis notebook workflows, using interactive Jupyter Widgets that work with Xenium, MERSCOPE, Visium HD, CosMx, and Chromium data.

Source code is on GitHub.

docs.title: Learn More
docs.text:
• Visualizations - The spatial, data, and info widgets Celldega provides
  • Getting Started Guide - Quick start with installation and examples
  • Installation - Detailed installation instructions
  • File Formats - Understanding LandscapeFiles

docs.title: Celldega File Formats
docs.text:
While there has been tremendous progress in developing standardized data formats and architectures for spatial-omics data, namely SpatialData and the related AnnData, these approaches currently lack support for interactive cloud-based visualization of large (>100M transcripts) Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) data. Furthermore, all-in-one data format approaches preclude the development of compact visualization-specific data formats.

The Celldega project addresses these challenges with the development of a new ST data format called LandscapeFiles, specifically built for cloud-based visualization. LandscapeFiles support Celldega's Landscape visualization method by leveraging compact image formats and cloud-native data formats to enable efficient storage and visualization of image (e.g., microscopy images) and vectorized data (e.g., transcript coordinates). This approach is highly scalable, enabling the visualization of very large ST datasets (>400M transcripts), while remaining compact enough that the LandscapeFiles for an entire Xenium dataset can be hosted in a public GitHub repository.

docs.title: LandscapeFiles
docs.text: LandscapeFiles are generated using the Celldega pre module (see example Google Colab notebook Celldega-Landscape-Pre-Process_Xenium-Pancreas-Dataset) and are used by Celldega's JavaScript front-end to interactively visualize ST data. Users have several options for hosting LandscapeFiles both locally on the cloud (e.g., Terra.bio buckets) or locally (e.g., running a local server to locally host LandscapeFiles).

docs.title: iST LandscapeFiles
docs.text:
The file structure for a Xenium Prime dataset's LandscapeFiles is shown below.

.
├── cbg
├── cell_clusters
├── cell_metadata.parquet
├── cell_segmentation
├── df_sig.parquet
├── landscape_parameters.json
├── meta_gene.parquet
├── pyramid_images
│   ├── bound_files
│   ├── dapi_files
│   ├── prot_files
│   └── rna_files
│── transcript_tiles
└── micron_to_image_transform.csv

The LandscapeFiles for an an example public 10X Genomics Xenium dataset can be found here.

docs.title: Cell-by-Gene
docs.text:
The cbg directory contains parquet files for each gene. Each file has a table of all the non-zero single cell expression counts. See example below:

    A2ML1
aaaaljij-1  18
aaabgfcl-1  24
aaacghkb-1  28
aaachnfg-1  14
aaacknep-1  1

docs.title: Cell Clusters
docs.text: The cell_clusters directory contains single-cell clustering data. For Xenium data, these will include the default clustering results stored in two parquet files.

docs.title: cluster.parquet
docs.text:
This file contains the cluster identity of each cell. See example below:

    cluster
aaaaljij-1  28
aaabgfcl-1  27
aaacghkb-1  27
aaachnfg-1  28
aaacknep-1  28

docs.title: meta_cluster.parquet
docs.text:
This file contains metadata on the cell clusters, which includes the color and cell count. See example below:

    color   count
1   #1f77b4 12742
2   #ff7f0e 10058
3   #2ca02c 9171
4   #d62728 8781
5   #9467bd 7760

docs.title: Cell Metadata
docs.text:
The cell_metadata.parquet file contains the centroid positions of all cells. See example below:

cell_id name    geometry

aaaaljij-1  aaaaljij-1  [819.7626194690856, 10819.416697734863]
aaabgfcl-1  aaabgfcl-1  [861.7377139772034, 10683.254024123535]
